item.title: Xi's trip builds solidarity and consensus
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
Xi's trip builds solidarity and consensus Reforming, improving global governance also a key outcome, foreign minister says President Xi Jinping returned to Beijing on Thursday morning after attending the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek and concluding state visits to Kyrgyzstan and Egypt. Officials and experts said the five-day trip, covering more than 20 bilateral and multilateral events across Central Asia and the Middle East, responded to international calls for peace, stability and development with concrete efforts, offering Chinese solutions and insights to a world of intertwined changes and turbulence. Speaking at a news briefing in Cairo upon the conclusion of the trip, Foreign Minister Wang Yi said that with solidarity and cooperation as its central theme, the trip was significant for building consensus on cooperation and for reforming and improving global governance. In Bishkek, Xi attended the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the SCO as the organization marked its 25th anniversary this year. At the summit, Xi announced that China would establish a China-SCO port economic cooperation center in Tianjin and a China-SCO basic education cooperation center, and implement 100 technological cooperation projects with other SCO countries over the next three years. Leaders of the member states signed and issued the Bishkek Declaration, approved the protocol on amendments and additions to the SCO Charter, and adopted 28 outcome documents covering areas such as security, economic and people-to-people cooperation, as well as organizational development. The strategic blueprint drawn up at last year's Tianjin summit is becoming a reality step by step, Wang said, noting that the SCO now has a more optimized structure, more efficient operation and stronger cooperation. According to Wang, in Kyrgyzstan, the two heads of state reached important consensus on further deepening the two nations' comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era and advancing the building of a China-Kyrgyzstan community with a shared future. Bilateral relations are now at their best in history, he said. Wang said the most important political outcome of the visit was the signing of the treaty on permanent good-neighborliness, friendship and cooperation. The treaty enshrines the two countries' commitment to lasting friendship in legal form and opens broader prospects for bilateral relations, he said. Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Zheenbek Kulubaev told reporters that as a result of Monday's meeting of the heads of state, Kyrgyzstan and China have raised the strategic partnership to a high-quality level of development. This reflects the high level of political trust and confidence between the two countries and their readiness to further deepen cooperation, he said. Xi's trip to Egypt was the first state visit to the country by a Chinese president in a decade and coincided with the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations. According to Wang, Xi has emphasized that China, whether in the past, at present or in the future, is Egypt's trustworthy and dependable comprehensive strategic partner. Wang described Xi's historic visit to Egypt as both a journey to renew friendship and one to expand cooperation, calling it a milestone that fully demonstrates the strategic and exemplary nature of China-Egypt relations. Zoon Ahmed Khan, a researcher at the Belt and Road Institute of Tsinghua University, said Xi's visit reflected an ongoing transformation in which the two ancient civilizations are advancing from mere markets and transit corridors into creators of their own shared agency. "The true vitality of this partnership lies in its tangible momentum," she said, pointing to industrial hubs, local-currency financing, space technology and job-creating projects as examples of political trust being translated into productive capacity and practical South-South cooperation. Ayman Mohseb, a member of Egypt's House of Representatives, said that closer China-Egypt coordination could help ease regional tensions, promote dialogue and political settlements, and contribute to a more balanced and equitable international order. During his talks with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, Xi put forward a four-point proposal on building a new security architecture in the Middle East via upholding a vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security. He called for fostering the internal driving force for regional security, adopting a comprehensive approach to advancing common security in the region, consolidating the foundation for common security through development and strengthening international coordination. Wang also highlighted the cultural and people-to-people dimensions. Peng Liyuan, Xi's wife, took part in cultural activities with Aigul Japarova, the wife of the Kyrgyz president, and Entissar El-Sisi, the wife of the Egyptian president. The activities added a warm cultural dimension and helped strengthen mutual understanding, people-to-people bonds and cultural exchanges, Wang said. mojingxi@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Visitors tune in to melody road
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
When a visitor surnamed Zhang, from Shenyang, the capital of Liaoning province, took her family for a drive on a stretch of highway in North China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region, her car's tires began to hum a melody of the grasslands. "It was so much fun!" she recalled. "I had seen videos online, but experiencing it in person was completely different. The tires rolling over the road created this beautiful tune, and my first reaction was, 'Whoa, it really works!'" Zhang said she promptly turned around and drove along the stretch again. "It's just too short — I couldn't get enough of it." What this visitor experienced was the Dada Route's new "musical road" — an 800-meter stretch of road engineered to play a melody through friction when vehicles pass at a steady speed of no more than 50 kilometers per hour. Located near the western gate of the Asgat Stone Forest scenic area in Hexigten Banner in Inner Mongolia's Chifeng, the musical stretch of road features 12,366 grooves milled precisely in the asphalt. The "musical road" is the latest addition to the 135-km Dada Route, a highway that offers one of China's most scenic drives. The route winds its way through six distinct landscapes — lakes, grasslands, sandy areas, forests, mountains and the stone forest. It is often described as a "moving encyclopedia of the grassland". In 2024, the Dada Route was named one of China's most beautiful self-driving routes — the only highway in Inner Mongolia to receive the honor awarded by the Ministry of Transport. It now welcomes more than 3 million visitors and roughly 1 million vehicles each year. The journey begins at the serene Dalai Nuur Lake, one of Inner Mongolia's four largest inland lakes and a haven for migratory birds. As the road meanders through the vast Gongger Grassland, the landscape unfolds as an endless expanse of green dotted with grazing herds of cows, sheep and horses. The route culminates at the Asgat Stone Forest, a 5A-level scenic area — the highest category in China's five-tier tourist attraction rating system — and a world geological park. Formed more than 150 million years ago through volcanic eruptions and glacial movements, the stone forest features towering, layered granite pillars. Feng Litian, deputy director of the Hexigten Banner Culture, Tourism and Sports Bureau, said that since the "musical road" opened on June 1, around 420,000 trips have been recorded along the Dada Route. More than 80 percent of visitors to the area now arrive by car, he added.

item.title: Guangdong streamlines exit-entry procedures for visitors
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
Guangdong streamlines exit-entry procedures for visitors As Shenzhen prepares to host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in November, entry and exit procedures for foreign visitors across Guangdong province are being streamlined to ensure faster clearance. The number of visitors from Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation economies arriving in Guangdong's major cities, including Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Foshan and Dongguan, has risen steadily since the start of the year, reflecting deepening ties between APEC economies and the southern innovation and manufacturing hub, officials said. According to the Shenzhen General Station of Immigration Inspection, as of early August, foreign nationals entering and exiting Guangdong through Shenzhen's border ports had topped 5 million, a figure reached 58 days earlier than in 2025. Wu Sijue, a senior immigration inspection officer in Shenzhen, said that officers are working to improve port clearance efficiency, upgrade the digital arrival registration system, expand bilingual and multilingual services, and strengthen on-site consultation and passenger guidance. "We will open dedicated APEC lanes at eight ports, spanning airports, seaports, land ports and railway ports, and roll out tailored guidance and inspection measures to ensure safe, efficient and convenient clearance," Wu added. The Guangzhou General Station of Immigration Inspection said the demographic profile of the incoming visitors continues to diversify, driven by conventions, exhibitions, cultural tourism and other business activities. In the first half of the year, foreign nationals entering through ports administered by the station exceeded 2.02 million, up 32.9 percent year-on-year. Conference and business visitors accounted for 26.2 percent of all foreign arrivals, with the China Import and Export Fair, which is also known as the Canton Fair, being a core driver of this growth, it said. As a cross-border e-commerce hub, Guangzhou also attracts a steady stream of foreign sellers and logistics providers. As the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting approaches, presummit meetings for senior officials, a CEO summit and thematic working group sessions have brought waves of official delegations, business leaders and think tank experts, creating repeated visitor peaks, inspection officials said. Visa-exempt foreign arrivals accounted for more than half of all entries at Guangzhou's ports, and most of these were from APEC economies. The Zhuhai General Station of Immigration Inspection reported that foreign arrivals and departures through the city's ports had reached 1.46 million as of Aug 25. Among these, 310,000 entered under visa-exempt policies or with APEC business travel cards, accounting for more than 20 percent of all foreign arrivals. Han Yonghui, executive dean of the Guangdong Institute for International Strategies, attributed the sustained growth in APEC-related arrivals to visa facilitation, the momentum of the APEC "China Year", deep trade links with the Asia-Pacific region, expanded international connectivity, and improved urban services for inbound travelers. "Visa exemptions are the foremost driver," Han said, noting that strong trade, investment and industrial chain ties between Guangdong and APEC economies have created solid demand for recurring business travel, while a high-density air network has cut travel costs. The policy push is fueling strong interest among foreign visitors. French traveler Axel Jeremy Tom Beriel, who loves Chinese food, especially Cantonese cuisine, said he wants to see Guangdong's natural beauty, such as the mountains and forests, as well as the scenic landscapes surrounding the province's cities. "Chinese culture fascinates me too," he said. "There are so many time-honored, magnificent buildings and temples, and I'm eager to travel around and explore them all." Paul John Tomlins, a British traveler, said the entire customs clearance process was smooth and pleasant, adding that high-speed trains offer convenient transportation, allowing visitors to take in the scenery of different cities on a single trip.

item.title: HK's super connector role highlighted
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
HK's super connector role highlighted High-level officials and society leaders gathered in Hong Kong on Thursday for a major conference on integration of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, with keynote speakers highlighting the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region's role as a "super connector" between the Chinese mainland and global markets amid rapidly shifting geopolitical and technological landscapes. The conference, themed "New Dynamics in Asia-Pacific Cooperation, New Opportunities for GBA Connectivity", was co-organized by China Daily and the Hong Kong Coalition, bringing together nearly 300 government officials, consuls general, business leaders and representatives from think tanks, academia and media, as well as public-private sector experts from across Asia. Leung Chun-ying, vice-chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, said that collaborative initiatives unveiled recently in data and healthcare between Hong Kong and Nansha in Guangzhou, Guangdong province, underscore the unique role of Hong Kong as a partner and super connector linking the Greater Bay Area with the rest of the world. He said the steps to be taken are clear and necessary — to promote better government-to-business and business-to-business interactions between Hong Kong and Guangdong. "The new momentum generated in recent months through cooperation between Guangdong cities in the Greater Bay Area and Hong Kong will benefit other Asia-Pacific countries and regions," Leung said. Hong Kong SAR Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said in a video speech that the Greater Bay Area is fast becoming one of the most dynamic and integrated economic powerhouses in the world, underscoring Hong Kong's role as the only world city that converges both the China advantage and the global advantage. Lee said that this role takes on new significance this year, as the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen, Guangdong, in November, a historic first for the Greater Bay Area, and Hong Kong will host the APEC Finance Ministers' Meeting in October. He added that the region is ready for the spotlight. Lee said that Hong Kong has a deep and liquid market and a strong pool of financial and professional talent, and the city has become Asia's premier fundraising, asset management and risk management hub. He said the Hong Kong Park of the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone is key to turning cutting-edge ideas into tangible outcomes and world-class research into products, by bringing together Hong Kong's research excellence and the Chinese mainland's advanced manufacturing capabilities. He added that talent is central to Hong Kong's innovation and technology push, while highlighting the "one town, five elements" framework for the Northern Metropolis University Town Area — a hub where universities, research institutes and industries will be set up together to integrate the five elements of education, technology, talent, industry and urban development. "Integrating into and serving overall national development, Hong Kong brings together ideas, capital and talent across boundaries, and connects the Greater Bay Area with global markets. Together, we are not just building the Greater Bay Area. We are shaping a more connected, innovative and prosperous future," Lee said. Qu Yingpu, publisher and editor-in-chief of China Daily, said that the China Daily Hong Kong Edition has chronicled Hong Kong's remarkable voyage — enduring storms, celebrating triumphs and now recording a new era of transformation from stability to prosperity, aligned with the vibrant rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. "Amid shifting communication landscapes and unprecedented global change, we will continue to share the living story of and contribute to this 'one country, two systems', the dynamism of the Greater Bay Area and China's unwavering commitment to an open global economy," he said. Qu also said that he believes that Hong Kong will continue to innovate, leap forward and forge new heights of achievement with its first five-year plan, which is scheduled to be published on Sept 16. Hong Kong SAR Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po stressed connectivity and Hong Kong's role in connecting the world in an age of profound change driven by geopolitics and technological transformation. "As the country's most internationally connected region, the Greater Bay Area presents a strong value proposition for Asia-Pacific collaboration," Chan said. "It rests on a simple conviction: When we partner, we do not merely add up our strengths — we multiply them and extend their reach well beyond Asia." The conference also featured three panel discussions on Hong Kong's financial opportunities in the changing Asia-Pacific landscape, the synergy in commercial aerospace development between the HKSAR and Shenzhen, and education in the artificial intelligence era. Panelists highlighted how Hong Kong can seize opportunities arising from deeper Asia-Pacific economic and trade cooperation to enhance its influence as a global financial hub. Discussions also centered on harnessing the Greater Bay Area's manufacturing capabilities and Hong Kong's strengths, exploring ways to build a collaborative commercial space ecosystem. Panelists also examined how the education sector can reinvent its model with AI to cultivate talent that serves the Greater Bay Area and the Asia-Pacific market.

item.title: President calls for dialogue between civilizations
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
President calls for dialogue between civilizations President Xi Jinping emphasized the need for China and Egypt to jointly promote equality, dialogue, mutual learning and inclusiveness between civilizations during a visit to the Grand Egyptian Museum on Wednesday. Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, toured the museum accompanied by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and his wife, Entissar El-Sisi, before leaving Cairo for Beijing. The sprawling museum stands within sight of the Pyramids of Giza, and brings together some of the most important relics and artifacts from the ancient Egyptian civilization. Cultural exchanges between China and Egypt have flourished in recent years, from major exhibitions of ancient Egyptian artifacts in China to joint archaeological projects in Egypt. El-Sisi and his wife extended a warm welcome to Xi and Peng upon their arrival at the museum. They entered the main hall of the museum together and posed for a photo in front of the colossal monolith of King Ramesses II, before listening to an introduction to the museum and the history of ancient Egypt. They admired the exquisite stone statues, inscribed stone columns and a pyramidion from a temple, before stopping at the observation deck to take in the view of the pyramids in the distance. Xi and El-Sisi also visited the Tutankhamun Galleries, where they appreciated prized collections including the pharaoh's world-famous gold burial mask, gold throne and war chariots. Noting that China and Egypt are both ancient civilizations and countries rich in World Heritage sites, Xi said that across time and space, the two civilizations have been reaching out to each other and writing new chapters of everlasting friendship between the two peoples. Xi called on the two countries to uphold the vision of civilization based on equality, mutual learning, dialogue and inclusiveness, and implement the Global Civilization Initiative. He also urged both sides to promote inclusiveness, coexistence and mutual learning among different civilizations, thereby drawing greater strength from civilizations to advance the building of a community with a shared future for humanity. El-Sisi thanked Xi for sending a congratulatory message on the opening of the museum in Giza in November last year. He noted that ancient Egyptian and Chinese civilizations share the qualities of openness, inclusiveness and harmonious coexistence amid diversity, which closely aligns with the vision of the Global Civilization Initiative proposed by Xi. Egypt stands ready to strengthen people-to-people and cultural exchanges with China, promote mutual learning among civilizations, and help make the world more harmonious and inclusive, he said.

item.title: Language learning bridges Arab ties
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-03
Language learning bridges Arab ties On a trading floor inside Shishi clothing city in Fujian province, Egyptian businessman Hany Sobhy stood before a group of Chinese merchants, reading out Arabic words projected on a large screen during a free Arabic training course that he initiated. "Keef halik," he said, pointing to a row of seemingly odd Chinese characters — actually phonetic annotations designed to help his students pronounce the Arabic greeting correctly. "Al-alwan," he read, tracing the word for "colors". One by one, the students echoed him, reading the Arabic words aloud. The curriculum includes Arabic numerals, phrases for quantities and colors, packaging terms — "all practical business expressions", Sobhy explained. Thousands of miles away in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, young learners gather in smart classrooms for Chinese language sessions. In front of them, screens glow with audio links, animated clips and interactive games, while each desk is stocked with talking pens, flashcards and illustrated storybooks. As online tutors appear on the screens, local teachers stand by to provide face-to-face support. "Over 100 people inquire about our online Chinese courses daily. That shows just how popular learning Chinese has become across the Arab world," said Essam Audam Adam Ahamed, general manager of international marketing at Wisdom House International Culture Communication Group, a company dedicated to teaching Chinese to Arabic-speaking communities. "For young Arabs, learning Chinese used to be a hobby; now it is increasingly seen as a pathway to future careers," he said. "Learning Chinese opens up new opportunities." The surging enthusiasm for learning Chinese and Arabic stems from a shared desire to deepen mutual understanding between China and Arab states. For centuries, Chinese and Arab civilizations have connected through trade and people-to-people exchanges. Today, that connection is being rejuvenated amid the trend for learning each other's languages. Noting that language is the best key to understanding a country, President Xi Jinping said he is sincerely glad that the youths in Saudi Arabia have learned about a colorful, multidimensional and comprehensive China through learning Chinese. Learning each other's language and understanding each other's history and culture will help promote mutual understanding and bring the two peoples closer together, Xi said in a reply letter in 2022 to students learning Chinese. From barriers to bonds When Sobhy first came to China in 2015, he never expected that language would be such a huge barrier. He struggled to order meals at restaurants and negotiate with garment suppliers, relying entirely on hand gestures. Constant interactions with Chinese friends and business clients helped him gradually grasp the language. Today, he makes phone calls, sends text messages effortlessly in Chinese, and runs seven companies in China. Sobhy started teaching local merchants Arabic in 2019, when he found that most Arab buyers, like him at one time, spoke little Chinese or English. Among his students is Zheng Lang, an English-major-turned-merchant at Shishi clothing city, where clients mainly come from Arab states, South America and Central Asia. "Mastering the language gives me an upper hand," Zheng said. "At the very least, I can communicate smoothly and grasp their demands instantly." For Zheng, language has opened a door that leads not merely to business, but more importantly, mutual trust. Having worked in the garment trade for a decade, Zheng said her Arab clients all speak highly of made-in-China goods, saying that China is incredibly capable. As mutual trust has deepened between Chinese and Arab traders, a growing number of Arabs have flocked to the clothing city. Mohammed Alqubati, who earned his doctorate in mathematics in China, spotted untapped business opportunities amid this trend and opened a restaurant serving Arab cuisine. "Many new Arab merchants have no idea where to source factories, retail outlets and raw materials, so they often come to the restaurant for advice," Alqubati said, stressing that the venue has gradually become a hub for cultural exchanges, social gatherings and business negotiations. Both the clothing market and the Arab restaurant stand as vivid footnotes to the exchanges between China and Arab states over the past 70 years, a journey tracing back to 1956 when Egypt became the first Arab and African country to establish diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China. Ahmed Mustafa Fahmy, head of the League of Arab States' China representative office, said: "The China-Arab relationship is defined by a high degree of strategic mutual trust. This trust has been built not only over the past seven decades, but can be traced back to the era of the ancient Silk Road." The relationship between the two sides has always been characterized by mutual trust, mutual learning and mutual benefit, and there never have been strategic differences, he told China International Communications Group in a recent interview. Deeper understanding China has signed cooperation documents within the framework of the Belt and Road Initiative with all 22 Arab states and the League of Arab States. As the two sides continue to deepen cooperation across a wide range of sectors, observers have highlighted the role culture plays in bringing people together. Hussain bin Ibrahim Al Hammadi, ambassador of the United Arab Emirates to China, said that through education, language learning, publishing, artistic collaboration and academic exchanges, the two countries continue to strengthen the people-to-people connections that underpin long-term cooperation. "The true strength of any enduring partnership extends beyond economics. It is ultimately measured by the connections between people," he said in a signed article published by Global Times. Ahamed, the general manager at Wisdom House, expressed hope that more Arabs will learn Chinese, and more Chinese people will learn Arabic. "Language is one of the most beautiful bridges between civilizations. Through language, we get to know, understand and respect each other," he said. In recent years, a "Chinese language boom" has been taking place across the Arab world. From the Middle East to North Africa, Chinese language classrooms are multiplying. More than a dozen Arab countries have established Confucius Institutes, and an increasing number of Arab states, including the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Oman, have formally incorporated Chinese into their national education systems. Ahamed said that the demand for local professionals who are fluent in both Arabic and Chinese will keep rising, as numerous Chinese companies have set up operations across Arab states, covering the areas of energy, infrastructure and e-commerce. "That's why I believe learning Chinese means more job opportunities and broader career choices for young Arabs," he added. Besides Chinese language education, Zhang Shirong, chairman and founder of Wisdom House, said he has witnessed a clear rise in demand for Chinese books, films and TV series since the first China-Arab States Summit in 2022, as more people across the Arab world seek to learn more about China. "We have noted that political parties, prominent figures, scholars and students in Arab states are paying close attention to China's governance theories and practices," he said. "Among all the books we have sold, Xi Jinping: The Governance of China draws the greatest attention and ranks first in single-book sales," Zhang said. Ahamed said the company has set up Chinese language education institutes in 10 countries, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, Egypt and Libya. Calling language the finest bridge for mutual learning among civilizations, he laid out an ambitious target, saying that "our next goal is to roll out our programs to cover all 22 Arab states". Contact the writers at jihaisheng@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Brussels should resist the siren song of protectionism
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-03
Brussels should resist the siren song of protectionism The European Union worries about its trade deficit with China. But the remedy Brussels is reaching for risks making the problem worse. Maros Sefcovic, the European Commission's trade chief, plans a video call with Chinese officials this month and a visit to Beijing in October. He warned on Wednesday that the EU will impose "harsher measures" on China if trade talks do not produce "very concrete results", indicating the EU should restrain China's exports. That is a curious starting point for a trade negotiation. If Europe wants to narrow its deficit, it should first ask why its companies are exporting less — and what can be done to make them more competitive. China's manufacturing competitiveness reflects years of investment in research and development, fierce domestic competition, enormous economies of scale and the depth of an industrial ecosystem that allows companies to move rapidly from design to mass production. Europe has formidable strengths of its own. Its problem is that too many of its industries are losing ground in precisely the technologies and manufacturing capabilities that will determine future growth. Trade barriers will not repair that weakness. Instead, they will raise costs for European consumers and manufacturers that depend on Chinese inputs. With eurozone inflation already at 2.9 percent in July, above the European Central Bank's 2 percent target, restricting a source of relatively competitive goods is hardly cost-free. Protectionism can protect a producer while imposing a tax on everyone else. The EU's proposed carrot-and-stick approach — encouraging talks while threatening tougher measures — will not help address the EU's concerns. China today is a large technological and industrial economy with a huge domestic market and extensive trading relationships. Beijing will not accept a bargain in which dialogue is the carrot and coercion the stick. There is an even more important reason for Brussels to be cautious: it should not outsource its China policy to Washington. The recent G20 meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors in Asheville, North Carolina, offered a warning. Washington sought to rally partners around concerns about China's trade surplus and industrial "overcapacity", but the meeting ended without a communique amid disagreements. Europe knows this game well. The US has repeatedly portrayed the EU's trade surplus as justification for tariffs, forcing European governments to defend themselves against measures they regard as arbitrary. It would be self-defeating for Brussels to reject that logic when applied to Europe, only to reproduce it against China. France's so-called new anti-ultra-fast-fashion law illustrates the danger. The measure, taking effect this month, imposes escalating charges on low-cost fashion sold through platforms such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress, while many established European and traditional fast-fashion retailers face no equivalent burden. If environmental standards are the objective, they should be applied consistently rather than calibrated in ways that appear designed to hit particular foreign competitors. Such double standards invite precisely the World Trade Organization concerns that China has raised. The better route is to make trade more dynamically balanced by expanding Europe's capacity to sell, not simply restricting what it buys. That means reconsidering export controls on high-technology products, including machinery and equipment that European companies are capable of selling competitively in China; widening market access for European agricultural, automotive, pharmaceutical and medical-device producers; and tackling the regulatory and investment barriers that suppress European productivity. The trade and investment consultations mechanism established by China and the EU in June provides a mechanism for doing this. Brussels should use it to negotiate seriously over market access, subsidies, standards, industrial policy and the obstacles facing European exporters. Europe does not have to choose between Washington and Beijing. Nor should it imitate Washington in the hope of gaining leverage over Beijing. Its interest is simpler: a competitive European economy, open markets where they serve European interests, and trade rules applied consistently to all trading partners alike. The EU's trade deficit against China is a result of the EU's high-tech export restrictions and the law of the market. It didn't emerge overnight, and cannot be addressed by suppressing Chinese companies. The EU once recognized that protectionism was a threat to prosperity. It should not veneer it with virtue merely because Washington has rediscovered its swagger.

item.title: An ancient Chinese saying sheds light on our connected world
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-03
An ancient Chinese saying sheds light on our connected world Share - WeChat
What kind of world do we want to create? To explore this question, we begin with an ancient Chinese saying that has traveled across more than 1,600 years of history. “志合者不以山海为远” means "No mountain or ocean can distance people who have shared aspirations." The message behind the saying continues to resonate in today's interconnected world.
